changes.before: Save two meaningful commits and restore a deliberately broken change.
changes.after: Save chosen versions with Git so you can inspect changes and recover a mistake.

before: Git records versions you choose to save. A commit is a saved snapshot with a message explaining the change. Your working files can contain edits that are not committed. Staging selects the changes for the next commit; committing records that selection. Git does not automatically save every edit, and a local commit does not publish anything.

Use a disposable new folder called history-demo. Put a main.js file there that prints Hello. From its parent, this terminal sequence creates local history. Git must be installed, and the example identity is only for this disposable repository:
```bash
cd history-demo
git init
git config user.name "Practice Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.invalid"
git status
git add main.js
git commit -m "Add greeting"
```
init creates a repository; local config supplies an author identity; status shows file state. add stages main.js, and commit records that staged version with the supplied message.

Now edit main.js in your editor so it prints Hello, reader and save it. Run it to confirm the greeting, then use:
```bash
git diff
git add main.js
git commit -m "Improve greeting"
git log --oneline -2
```
diff shows unstaged changes. The second commit saves the improvement. log --oneline -2 shows the newest two commits as short identifiers and messages. Staging is a step before the commit; it does not delete old history.

For recovery practice, deliberately change that greeting to broken in this disposable file and save it. First inspect the difference and copy any uncommitted work you want to keep outside the file. Then run:
```bash
git status
git diff
git restore --source=HEAD -- main.js
node main.js
```
HEAD means the current commit. restore replaces this uncommitted file with HEAD's version; -- separates the file path from options. The program prints Hello, reader again. This discards the selected file's uncommitted change, so preserve wanted edits before restoring.

A committed mistake needs a different recovery. git revert with the mistake's commit id creates a new commit reversing it, preserving history. For example, in a disposable repository where the newest commit is the mistake, git revert HEAD reverses that commit and records the reversal. Review the chosen commit first; an older change can conflict with later work. Avoid destructive reset commands while learning this workflow.

For the exercise, restore returns a copy of the last versions entry. The supplied history has two entries, so the latest code is Hello, coder and the original first entry remains Hello. The function assumes a nonempty history, as supplied. Finish the local Git task as well: inspect two meaningful commits, recover one uncommitted mistake, and rerun the restored program. The browser model cannot establish that real Git history exists on your computer.
after: Git keeps versions of a project. A commit is a saved version with a message. Staging chooses the changes for the next commit. A local commit stays on your computer until you share it.

With Git installed, make a new disposable history-demo folder. Add main.js that prints Hello. From the parent folder, run this example. The sample author settings apply only to this practice project.

```bash
cd history-demo
git init
git config user.name "Practice Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.invalid"
git status
git add main.js
git commit -m "Add greeting"
```

add stages the file. commit saves that staged version. status shows what is saved, staged, or changed.
Edit main.js to print Hello, reader. Save and run it. Use git diff to inspect the change, then git add main.js and git commit -m "Improve greeting". git log --oneline -2 shows the two latest commits.

In this disposable file, change the greeting to broken without committing it. Inspect git diff and separately save anything you want to keep. Then git restore --source=HEAD -- main.js replaces the file with its last committed version. Run it to check the recovered greeting.
HEAD names the current commit. If a mistake was already committed, git revert can make a new commit that reverses it. Check the chosen commit before reverting it; later changes may need care.
The browser exercise models history as an array. Complete restore(history) by copying its last entry. The last index is history.length - 1. Object spread makes a new object for its flat fields.
The supplied history is nonempty. Return the latest version without changing earlier entries. Separately check that your local Git project has two commits and that the restored file runs.

before.question: You run git add main.js but have not run git commit. Has this created a recorded commit?
choices: Yes; add creates the commit immediately
Yes; add also publishes the change online
No; the changes are staged for a later commit
before.explanation: Staging selects changes for the next commit. Recording and publishing history are separate steps.

after.question: You run git add main.js but have not run git commit. Is there a new commit?
choices: Yes. add saves a commit immediately.
Yes. add also publishes it online.
No. The change is staged for the next commit.
after.explanation: Staging chooses changes. Committing records them as a version.
